Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of three numbers does not change their sum: adding the first two and then the third is equivalent to adding the last two and then the first. In floating-point arithmetic, however, every intermediate result usually must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Since rounding occurs after each operation, changing the grouping can change which intermediate values are rounded and therefore change the final result.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes or when positive and negative terms nearly cancel. If a very small number is added to a much larger number, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear entirely. If several small numbers are added together first, their combined value may become large enough to affect the larger number. Thus, the same inputs can produce slightly different sums solely because they were processed in a different order. IEEE 754 arithmetic defines formats and rounding behavior, but it does not make addition associative.

Large matrix multiplications contain many such additions. Each output element is a dot product formed by multiplying corresponding entries and reducing the products into a sum. High-performance implementations rarely perform that reduction in one fixed, simple left-to-right order. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work across processor cores or graphics-processing-unit threads, accumulate partial sums in registers, and combine those partial sums through reduction trees. Different thread schedules, tile sizes, vector widths, library algorithms, or hardware architectures can therefore produce different reduction orders.

Because each order creates a different sequence of rounded intermediate results, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications may differ in their low-order bits. Fused multiply-add instructions can also affect results because they compute a multiplication and addition with a single rounding rather than rounding both operations separately. The discrepancies are usually small, but they can grow when dot products are long, data are poorly scaled, or cancellation is severe. They may also propagate through later stages of a numerical algorithm or machine-learning computation.

Consequently, repeated executions are not necessarily bit-for-bit reproducible, particularly when parallel scheduling or algorithm selection is nondeterministic. Results may still be numerically valid within an appropriate error tolerance, but exact equality tests can fail. Stronger reproducibility requires fixed reduction trees, deterministic library settings, consistent hardware and compiler behavior, or more accurate accumulation methods such as higher-precision, compensated, or exact summation. These measures generally impose costs in performance, memory use, or implementation complexity.
